A free market is incredibly difficult to impossible in health care because of several reasons. To contrast with steel, if you need a particular grade of steel, it doesn't matter if you get it from India, the U.S.A., Uzbekistan, or wherever. It's always going to be just that. A doctor, on the other hand, may diagnose you differently, perform their surgeries in a different way, prescribe different medication. In addition, you may react differently to any one of those things. What's good for the goose is not necessarily good for the gander in those cases.

In addition, in a true free market, you can walk away from a deal if you don't like the terms and just deal with it. No one is going to walk away from a triple bypass and just deal with it, because the alternative is dying.

Beyond even that, we have to deal with things like information asymmetry, which is yet another market failure. Doctors can recommend unnecessary care to pad their bottom line, even though it might not help the patient at all. Maybe a drug over a different one not because of benefit to the consumer, but because of financial relation to the producer. Patients don't have the knowledge to know if they're getting solid advice, especially when that's compounded by the first issue I mentioned. Another doctor may just recommend things to pad their bottom line, so even getting a second opinion may not be viable.

IMO if we really wanted to provide universal health care we'd do two things- Repeal the limitation on Medicare part D for negotiating drug costs, and put everyone on Medicare (which would include any necessary tax changes to allow for that.). Ultimately this changes the balance of power in cost negotiation because local providers can no longer flex their monopolies, since they're not the biggest player in that negotiation. Allowing Medicare to negotiate drug costs will help curb the absolutely insane high costs of some medications owing to that same big stick.
